title: MedicaCore - Air-gapped On‑Prem Deployment & GPU Driver / Artifact Flow Deep Dive
summary: Deep technical session focused on on-prem, air-gapped delivery model: artifact packaging and signing, offline licensing, GPU driver matrix, container runtime choices, KV cache warm-starting, batching tradeoffs, and acceptance test plan for pilot.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-03-14 15:00 UTC | Duration: 63 mins | Recording: yes
Attendees: Sara Kim (Redwood AE), Dmitri Volkov (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Dr. Elena Park (MedicaCore), Luis Ramirez (MedicaCore CTO), Aisha Khan (MedicaCore Sec), Tom Becker (MedicaCore SRE)

[00:00] Sara: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time. Quick round of intros? We did a short pre-call but want to make sure we capture the infra folks.
[00:06] Elena: Hi, Elena Park, I run infra for MedicaCore. We're responsible for the on‑prem cluster and compliance for PHI workloads.
[00:10] Luis: Luis Ramirez, CTO, I'll be listening in for the architecture and procurement implications.
[00:13] Aisha: Aisha Khan, security architect. Focus on attestation, keys, audit.
[00:16] Tom: Tom Becker, SRE. I'll handle runtime and driver installs.
[00:19] Sara: Great. From Redwood: I'm Sara (AE), Dmitri and Priya are our SEs who will lead the technical bits. We'll walk through artifact delivery, licensing, and GPU driver compatibility and then sync on pilot next steps.
[00:29] Dmitri: Thanks. Wanted to set expectations: this is an air‑gapped installation pattern we've done a handful of times. Two common models: 1) shipping signed OCI images into an offline registry and 2) shipping a pre-built tarball + signed manifests we untar into /opt/redwood. Each has implications for updates, attestations, and how we handle the KV cache checkpointing.
[00:46] Tom: Quick clarification — when you say OCI images into offline registry, you mean a private harbor or Azure registry behind firewall that we seed from a jumpbox?
[00:52] Priya: Exactly; you seed via a jumpbox. For some customers we provide a signed SBOM and the signed image manifest so your security team can verify checksums.
[00:59] Aisha: We need proof of provenance. We can't accept unsigned artifacts. What does Redwood provide for signing?
[01:04] Dmitri: We sign images/manifests with our code signing cert and provide a detached signature file. For tarball workflows we provide an HMAC and a PGP signature you can verify offline. We also include an SBOM in CycloneDX format.
[01:13] Aisha: Good. Also we need offline attestations for the install bundle — something we can archive for audits.
[01:19] Priya: We include an install manifest with checksums, drift detection hashes, and a generated install receipt that you can store in your artifact repository. We can also provide an offline verification tool that runs in your air‑gapped environment to check signatures.
[01:29] Elena: Sounds promising. Now, GPU drivers — we run a mix of A100s and older V100s. What's your tested driver matrix? We've had pain with driver versions breaking container runtimes.
[01:38] Dmitri: Right. Short answer: supported NVIDIA driver versions are 525.x and 535.x for our CUDA 12 builds; for older CUDA 11 stacks (V100) we support 470.x. We test against the NVIDIA container toolkit and nvidia‑dali stacks. We'll provide a compatibility matrix and a small smoke test to validate nvml and CUDA visible devices.
[01:55] Tom: Do you require a specific container runtime? We're on runc + containerd, not docker‑engine.
[02:01] Priya: containerd + runc is fine. We also support CRI‑O in our on‑prem package. The important bit is the host NVIDIA container toolkit and matching driver. We provide a shim that loads GPU libraries into the container.
[02:11] Luis: Is there a recommended kernel version? We try to stay LTS kernel 5.15 for compatibility with some of our appliances.
[02:16] Dmitri: Kernel 5.15 is OK for the driver versions above; we'll flag any kernel modules we build. We'll supply the exact dkms module versions if you prefer building on host.
[02:26] Elena: About licensing — we are air‑gapped and also under a procurement model that needs offline activation. How does Redwood do licensing for on‑prem?
[02:33] Sara: We have an offline licensing flow. You supply a hardware fingerprint (we prefer a host manifest containing GPU UUIDs + MAC addresses + cluster ID). We generate a time‑bound license file signed by Redwood that you drop into /etc/redwood/license.key. No external calls required at runtime.
[02:45] Aisha: Is the license tied to a specific GPU UUID? What about hardware replacement during the pilot?
[02:50] Dmitri: We can issue licenses with a range of allowed GPU UUIDs or with a grace window for hardware swaps. For pilot, we typically provide a 30‑day grace policy. For long term, we can issue a replacement process that involves a new signed license after verification of the new hardware manifest.
[03:03] Aisha: Auditability — can we get a signed statement from Redwood if we need to demonstrate licensing compliance?
[03:08] Sara: Yes, we can provide a signed license ledger export and a vendor attestation letter for procurement.
[03:14] Tom: Back to artifacts — if we untar to /opt/redwood, how are updates applied? We have strict change windows.
[03:20] Priya: We provide an offline patch bundle that includes delta patches (binary diffs) and a patch runner that applies updates atomically and writes an install receipt. The patch runner supports dry‑run verification so you can test installs in a local staging host.
[03:34] Luis: For the runtime itself: how does your serving runtime handle KV cache warm starts? We need cold start behavior minimized because of real‑time use.
[03:42] Dmitri: We support checkpointing of KV cache and continuous incremental snapshots. For air‑gapped, we recommend pre‑warming with a load generator that replays common prefixes to populate the KV. We can also provide a serialized KV snapshot file that you can seed on startup. That file's size depends on the model and typical prefix length.
[03:57] Elena: What's the size ballpark? For a 7B model with 32k context and our prefix set, what are we looking at?
[04:03] Dmitri: Roughly 1.5–3GB for warm KV per replica for 7B if you're keeping a modest set of prefixes; for 70B it scales more. The snapshot is compressed and we recommend using our chunked format over the network or on USB.
[04:17] Tom: If we use snapshots, how do you handle version mismatches when we patch the runtime or quantize?
[04:22] Priya: Snapshots are tagged with runtime and model version. When there's a mismatch, the loader rejects or migrates snapshots; migration is allowed in most minor runtime patch cases but not when model architecture or tokenizer changes. We surface clear error codes in the startup logs.
[04:34] Aisha: On quantization — we plan to quantize for cost. How do you present quantization profiles for QA? We can't accept major accuracy regressions for clinical text.
[04:42] Dmitri: We produce quantization profiles per model with measured deltas on your supplied eval set. For on‑prem, we suggest a small canary: run your PII-sensitive prompts against quantized and FP16/FP32 variants in a controlled environment. We'll provide eval harness output and per‑prompt delta.
[04:56] Elena: Do you do per‑token soft fallback? Like if quantized model confidence drops we route to a higher precision variant?
[05:02] Dmitri: We support model‑level fallback (route to FP32/FP16 variant) per request. We don't do per‑token hybrid generation yet. But batching and routing policies can be set to prefer lower‑cost variants unless a request is flagged for higher precision.
[05:13] Sara: That metric gating is often done via your app layer flagging certain request types as "sensitive" or "high‑accuracy". We can integrate with your routing policies.
[05:22] Luis: On batching: we have 100ms latency targets for interactive features. How does Redwood's batching affect tail latency?
[05:28] Dmitri: Our continuous batching aims to keep latency under SLO by creating small, time‑bounded batches. For 100ms target, we recommend max batch delay of 6–8ms and batch size caps tuned to your QPS. There's a tradeoff: larger batches lower cost but increase p95. We can provide a tuning matrix after we see traffic shape.
[05:47] Tom: Can we disable batching per route? Some routes must be strictly single‑token p50 < 60ms.
[05:52] Priya: Yes, batching configs are per‑route. You can set batching to "latency‑first" or "throughput‑first". Also prefix caching reduces token compute for repeated prefixes which helps meet low latency.
[06:05] Elena: About prefix cache — how persistent is it across restarts? Does it require redis or a local disk store?
[06:10] Dmitri: The KV checkpoint persists to disk and can be backed by local SSD. For multi‑host coordination we use a durable store in your network — some customers use an on‑prem MinIO or NFS. But in air‑gapped setups we support standalone node persistence for the cache.
[06:22] Aisha: Encryption at rest requirements — we need the cached data encrypted with customer‑managed keys.
[06:27] Sara: We support customer KMS via HSM exports: you can give us a public key to encrypt the snapshot chunks, or we can integrate with on‑prem HSM to decrypt at runtime. For archive, we produce encrypted tarballs.
[06:36] Luis: If snapshots are encrypted with customer keys, is there any runtime overhead for decrypting?
[06:40] Dmitri: Negligible if we use a streaming decryptor and chunk sizes tuned. Decrypt is CPU bound but minimal compared to GPU inference. We'll include benchmarks in the driver compatibility doc.
[06:52] Tom: Drivers again — do you require a specific Nvidia kernel module or provisioned nvidia‑persistenced?
[06:57] Priya: We recommend enabling nvidia‑persistenced for faster cold starts. We also supply a systemd unit that ensures the right module loads before the runtime. In some environments we provide a prebuilt dkms package to avoid manual compiles.
[07:10] Elena: For the air‑gapped install itself, what's the install time expectation for a 4 node cluster?
[07:15] Dmitri: From your side, tarball unpack + preflight + runtime install should be under 90 minutes with an experienced sysadmin. Seed time for KV warmup depends on snapshot size — could be 10–45 minutes.
[07:27] Luis: Benchmarks — can we run local perf tests? We want to check throughput/latency at 95/99.
[07:33] Dmitri: Yes. We provide a benchmarking script that runs in your environment. It produces p50/p95/p99 numbers for token latency, throughput per GPU, and end‑to‑end tail latency with different batching and sequence lengths. The script's results are deterministic given same driver and CUDA.
[07:47] Tom: Are the benchmarks validated by Redwood or provided raw? We prefer raw plus a Redwood run for comparison.
[07:53] Priya: We'll ship the raw harness and can run a Redwood controlled run in a mirror environment; we'll provide both output files and a normalized comparison.
[08:03] Aisha: Compliance: SOC2 evidence — you mentioned earlier audit logs and install receipts. Will those be included in the on‑prem package?
[08:10] Sara: Yes. The built package includes audit logging components that log control plane actions (deployments, rollbacks, license installs). Logs are written to your local ELK or SIEM endpoints. We also deliver a compliance pack with process docs.
[08:21] Elena: How do we revoke a license if something goes wrong?
[08:24] Dmitri: License revocation in air‑gapped is handled via a revocation list you can load from a signed file. For urgent revocation you can request a signed revocation bundle from Redwood which you install via the jumpbox.
[08:35] Sara: Ok quick pivot to acceptance criteria for pilot so procurement knows what to sign: 1) runtime deploys on two node cluster, 2) runs benchmark and meets p95 < 200ms for our sample scenario, 3) KV snapshot seed works and persists across restart, 4) offline license installed and verified, 5) audit logs generated.
[08:55] Luis: That sounds reasonable. Can you map those to pass/fail items?
[09:00] Priya: We'll produce a one‑page acceptance checklist and a small test harness. We'll also provide an SRE runbook.
[09:08] Aisha: Security review — we need to scan the SBOM. Does Redwood allow us to run our own SCA on the images?
[09:15] Dmitri: Absolutely. We provide the CycloneDX SBOM and signed manifests; you can run your own SCA tools. If any transitive dependencies are flagged we can patch and reissue signed images.
[09:25] Tom: In the event of GPU driver security patches, is there an offline channel for CVE patches?
[09:30] Sara: Yes, we prepare a patch bundle and communicate CVE severity. For critical patches we can push an emergency patch bundle and provide instructions for quick apply.
[09:38] Elena: Operational question: Can we run Redwood as a non‑privileged user? We have policies to minimize root processes.
[09:44] Dmitri: The runtime requires limited privileges to access /dev/nvidia* devices; however, we can run the server under a dedicated low‑privilege service account if device nodes are properly chowned and setcap is configured. We document least privilege setups in the install guide.
[09:57] Luis: A quick callout on observability — how granular are your trace IDs and request logs? We need correlation with our APM.
[10:03] Priya: We emit request IDs, span traces, and token‑level timing samples. You can forward traces to Jaeger/OpenTelemetry collector on‑prem. Logs are JSON and structured for easy ingest.
[10:13] Tom: Let's talk about network topology. Do you require outbound connectivity for any part of the runtime?
[10:18] Dmitri: For pure air‑gapped installs: none. For optional analytics telemetry if you opt‑in, we use an outbound endpoint. The default is telemetry‑off.
[10:28] Aisha: What about license renewal notifications — we need them to be offline too.
[10:31] Sara: We'll provide a license ledger you host. We can create an offline calendar file or a signed file you can check against. Also our AE will send renewal notices via email to the procurement contact—human process.
[10:42] Luis: Ok, time to surface risk areas for our board: hardware replacement, patching windows, and initial warmup costs. Any mitigation suggestions?
[10:50] Priya: For hardware swap we recommend a documented replacement playbook and a rolling license reissue process. For patching, we suggest a blue/green deploy pattern in your cluster. For warmup costs, we recommend seeding with conservative prefix selection and measuring the incremental benefit. We'll help model cost vs latency.
[11:06] Tom: One practical item — what exact files do we need to give you for the hardware fingerprint?
[11:10] Dmitri: A single tar gz containing: nvidia‑smi --query‑gpu=gpu_uuid,index and MAC list (ip link show) and a cluster id file. Hash that and send the sha256. We'll provide an offline uploader CLI but if you prefer a zipped manifest via SFTP to our secure intake we can do that.
[11:25] Elena: We operate under strict PHI rules; anything that leaves network has to be fully encrypted and accompanied by export controls.
[11:32] Sara: Understood. Our transport supports AES‑GCM and PGP wrapped payloads. We also support FIPS modules where necessary.
[11:40] Luis: Any third‑party components that are problematic in air‑gapped envs? For example, some inference runtimes rely on cloud native image signing services.
[11:48] Dmitri: We avoid cloud signing services for air‑gapped installs. All signing is done by Redwood with artifacts delivered as signed bundles. We have a verifier binary so your team can locally confirm signatures.
[11:57] Aisha: About SSO for on‑prem console — does that require outbound calls? We prefer SAML with your IdP via SAML metadata exchange.
[12:03] Priya: We support SAML and can work with AD FS, Okta via metadata exchange during setup. That metadata exchange is done offline with signed metadata XML. No runtime outbound calls required.
[12:14] Tom: Let's capture the concrete deliverables for the pilot.
[12:17] Sara: We'll provide: 1) install tarball with signed manifest and SBOM, 2) driver/compatibility matrix and smoke tests, 3) KV snapshot for seeding, 4) offline license file, 5) benchmarking harness and acceptance checklist, 6) runbook and patch bundle.
[12:32] Luis: Timeline? If procurement signs next week, when can we start the pilot?
[12:36] Sara: Target: package delivery within 5 business days after we receive hardware manifest and PO. Onsite or remote install in the following week.
[12:43] Elena: Can we get a hardened install option that avoids persistent admin shells?
[12:47] Dmitri: Yes, we have a hardened profile that disables interactive shells and hardens the control plane. We'll provide CIS‑style checklist.
[12:56] Aisha: One more question — logs retention. We need 7 years for some audit trails. Is that feasible?
[13:01] Priya: The runtime writes to your storage; retention policy is yours. We can set log rotation guidance; storage size scales accordingly.
[13:09] Sara: Ok, we should recap next steps. Dmitri, Priya — will you own the technical deliverables?
[13:14] Dmitri: Yes, we'll own the matrix, snapshot, and the benchmarking harness.
[13:18] Priya: I'll own the runbook, install runner, and patch bundles.
[13:22] Sara: I'll own commercial items and the license file creation flow.
[13:25] Luis: Great. Aisha will do the security review once we get artifacts. Tom and I will run the pilot.
[13:30] Elena: Anything else?
[13:31] Tom: Small ask: can we get a short demo of the preflight smoke test? If not today, a short recorded demo.
[13:35] Dmitri: Yes, we'll share a 10 minute video of running preflight and checking nvml devices.
[13:40] Sara: Cool. We'll follow up with the acceptance checklist, PM timeline, and a signed SOW template. Thanks everyone.
[13:46] (end)

Transcription notes: occasional mis‑hearings corrected where obvious. Some acronyms spelled out (SBOM, NVML). There are a few filler words and brief crosstalk.

Schedule pilot install window once artifacts exchanged
